newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY TO SELL LARGE COMPANIES IN 1997 - MINISTER.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY TO SELL LARGE COMPANIES IN 1997 - MINISTER.

text.p: Hungary's privatisation minister says foreign investors will be offered stakes in several large Hungarian industrial and transport companies and banks this year.
Judit Csiha spoke with journalists ahead of her visit to Britain on Sunday, where she will meet government leaders and inform investors about investment opportunities in Hungary.
"Privatisation has arrived at its last phase," she said. "We will invite bids this year for the assets which the state does not want to keep."
Csiha said Hungary would be pleased to see British and overseas investors bidding for shares in the national electricity company Magyar Villamos Muvek Rt (MVM).
Investors mainly from Germany and France already hold large stakes in Hungary's energy distribution companies, while Belgian, Italian and British firms have bought into the power generation sector.

Csiha said that the government was likely to approve the MVM's privatisation plan by June, adding that the Paks nuclear station and the electricity transmission-line firm OVIT, both MVM subsidiaries, were not likely to be separated from the parent company.
She said the government will probably decide on the sales plan of shares in the truck maker company Raba in two weeks.
"I expect a combination of (sales to) financial and strategic investors."
The minister expects the privatisation of the national air carrier Malev to continue towards the end of the year, after closing negotiations with Alitalia , a minority shareholder in Malev.

Hungary also plans to sell a further stake in the oil and gas company MOL between March and June and the government is likely to discuss privatisation plans of the state shipping company Mahart in the near future, Csiha said.
She added banks, such as Kereskedelmi and Hitelbank (K&H), Mezobank and Takarekbank, would be sold this year.

Hungary will need substantial foreign investments in the next ten years, she said, adding that she would also call the attention of her British negotiating partners to investment opportunities in Hungary following the close of privatisation.
"We would like to get partners for the development of assets which the state will continue to manage," she said. "This also means green field investments and cooperation in joint ventures."
